1.title: Hooks, Secrets and Key Management
1.text: Welcome to Module fourteen: Hooks, Secrets and Key Management. This module covers the skills claude hooks, identity, secrets and key management. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do three things. Hooks as guardrails that prevent destructive actions. Identity validation and authentication, access approval, and authorized access monitoring. Managing secrets, credentials and A P I (application programming interface) keys in development and production.

1.title: Case Check-In: Tidewater's Coding Agent Almost Deletes a Folder
1.text: Our running case is Tidewater Insurance. Tidewater's Coding Agent Almost Deletes a Folder. An engineer's Claude Code session runs shell commands to clean up files. One command would have removed a shared directory. The team wants a rule that always holds, even when the model makes a mistake.

1.title: Hooks as Guardrails
1.text: Hooks as Guardrails. Hooks run your code at fixed points of the agent loop, outside the model, so they give deterministic guarantees that prompt text cannot. Pre Tool Use. When: Before a tool runs. Typical guardrail use: Deny destructive commands (rm -rf, force pushes, writes to.env or production paths), require confirmation, or rewrite arguments. Post Tool Use. When: After a tool returns. Typical guardrail use: Log for audit, redact secrets from output, normalize results. Prompt submit or stop. When: Around the prompt or the end of a turn. Typical guardrail use: Add context, validate the final state.

1.title: Hooks as Guardrails, continued
1.text: Hooks as Guardrails, continued. A blocking hook can deny a call (a deny decision with a reason, or exit code two for command hooks); the model sees the reason and tries something safer. Configure hooks in settings.json (shared project settings for the team, user settings for you) or in the Agent S D K (software development kit) hooks option; use a matcher to target tools such as Bash or Write Edit. Hooks versus permissions versus prompts: permission rules allow, ask or deny tools by pattern; hooks add custom logic (inspect arguments, call a policy service); prompts only suggest. For destructive-action prevention, use hooks and permission rules.

1.title: Hooks as Guardrails, continued
1.text: Hooks as Guardrails, continued. The figure shows this: A Pre Tool Use hook blocks destructive commands before they run; a Post Tool Use hook logs and redacts afterwards. Exam tip: "The agent must never run X" to a Pre Tool Use hook or deny rule; "log every tool call" to a Post Tool Use hook. Hooks do not make the model wiser: they stop actions. Exam tip: A keyed browser or mobile app is a leaked key: route calls through your server.

1.title: Identity, Secrets and Key Management
1.text: Identity, Secrets and Key Management. Identity validation and authentication. Verify who is calling: your users authenticate to your application; your application authenticates to Claude with an A P I key (first-party) or cloud identity (I A M roles on Bedrock, service accounts on Google Cloud). Access approval and level verification. Check what that identity may do before acting; separate roles; require approval for high-privilege actions. Authorized access monitoring. Log and review who accessed what; alert on unusual use; track A P I usage per key and workspace.

1.title: Identity, Secrets and Key Management, continued
1.text: Identity, Secrets and Key Management, continued. Secrets management. A P I keys and credentials live in a secrets manager or environment variables, never in source code, prompts, logs or client-side code. Key handling. Keys start with sk-ant- and are shown once at creation; store them immediately; set an expiration; use separate keys per environment and service; rotate regularly and revoke on suspicion. Key types. Prefer personal or service-account keys (tied to an owner, stop working when the account is removed) over a legacy workspace key. Least privilege. Scope keys to the workspace and use cloud I A M roles limited to the allowed models.

1.title: Identity, Secrets and Key Management, continued
1.text: Identity, Secrets and Key Management, continued. The figure shows this: Keep secrets in a secrets manager, inject them as environment variables, rotate them, and never place them in source code, prompts, logs or browser code. If a key leaks: revoke it, rotate to a new one, remove it from history, and review usage for abuse. Never call the A P I directly from a browser or mobile app with an embedded key: route requests through your server, which holds the key and enforces the user's permissions.

1.title: Identity, Secrets and Key Management, continued
1.text: Identity, Secrets and Key Management, continued. Do not put secrets in prompts or tool results: they can leak through output or injection (Module thirteen). Use the S D K's environment variable (A N T H R O P I C A P I K E Y) support so keys stay out of code. Exam tip: Hooks stop actions; they do not make the model's reasoning better. Pair them with permission rules.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Hooks: Run outside the model: Pre Tool Use (deny, ask, rewrite), Post Tool Use (log, redact). Block: Deny decision with a reason (or exit code two for command hooks). Where: settings.json (shared project for the team) or Agent S D K hooks option. Hooks versus prompts: Hooks and permission rules enforce; prompts suggest. Keys: sk-ant-,; shown once; secrets manager or env var; expire, separate, rotate, revoke. Never: In code, prompts, logs, git or client-side code. Identity: Users authenticate to your app; app authenticates to Claude (A P I key or cloud I A M). Monitoring: Log and review access; track usage per key and workspace.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A coding agent must never execute commands that delete shared directories, even if the model proposes them. Which control fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. A pre-execution hook enforces the rule deterministically; prompts only suggest.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A team wants a record of every tool call and its result, with secrets removed. Which hook fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. A post-tool hook sees the result and can log and transform it.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A developer pastes the production A P I key into the front-end Java Script of a customer portal. What is the right fix? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Keys must never be client-side; a server should call the A P I on behalf of authenticated users.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Where should an A P I key live for a deployed service? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Secrets stay out of code and prompts and are injected securely per environment.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Select two. Which two are good key management practices? The five options are on the screen. The answers are C and E. Separation, rotation, expiration and owned keys limit risk; sharing, committing and logging keys do the opposite.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all five answers. Question one: A. Question two: C. Question three: A. Question four: C. Question five: C and E. In the next module, we continue the course.
